title: Gene Wilder
wiki_lead:
Gene Wilder (born Jerome Silberman; June 11, 1933 – August 29, 2016) was an American actor, comedian, writer and filmmaker. He was most notable for his comedic roles, including his collaborations with Mel Brooks on the films The Producers (1967), Blazing Saddles and Young Frankenstein (both 1974), and with Richard Pryor in the films Silver Streak (1976), Stir Crazy (1980), See No Evil, Hear No Evil (1989) and Another You (1991), as well as his portrayal of Willy Wonka in Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory (1971).
He began his career on stage, and made his screen debut in an episode of the television series The Play of the Week in 1961. His first film role was that of a hostage in the 1967 motion picture Bonnie and Clyde. His first major film role was as Leopold Bloom in the 1967 film The Producers, for which he was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor. It was the first in a series of collaborations with writer/director Mel Brooks, including Young Frankenstein, which Wilder co-wrote, garnering the pair an Academy Award nomination for Best Adapted Screenplay. He also starred in Woody Allen's Everything You Always Wanted to Know About Sex* (*But Were Afraid to Ask) (1972).
Wilder directed and wrote several of his own films, including The Woman in Red (1984). With his third wife, Gilda Radner, he starred in three films, the last two of which he also directed. Her 1989 death from ovarian cancer led to his active involvement in promoting cancer awareness and treatment, helping found the Gilda Radner Ovarian Cancer Detection Center in Los Angeles and co-founding Gilda's Club. After his last acting performance in 2003—a guest role on Will & Grace, for which he received a Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Guest Actor in a Comedy Series—Wilder turned his attention to writing. He produced a memoir, Kiss Me Like a Stranger (2005) and five other books.

Early life and education
Wilder was born Jerome Silberman on June 11, 1933, in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, to a Russian Jewish family. He was the son of Jeanne (née Baer) and William J. Silberman, a manufacturer and salesman of novelty items. Wilder first became interested in acting at age eight, when his mother was diagnosed with rheumatic fever and the doctor told him to "try and make her laugh."
At the age of 11, he saw his sister, who was studying acting, performing onstage, and the experience enthraled him. He asked her teacher if he could become his student, and the teacher said that if he was still interested at age 13, he would take Wilder on as a student. The day after Wilder turned 13, he called the teacher, who accepted him; Wilder studied with him for two years.
When Jeanne Silberman felt that her son's potential was not being fully realized in Wisconsin, she sent him to Black-Foxe, a military institute in Hollywood, where he was bullied and sexually assaulted, primarily because he was the only Jewish boy in the school, according to his own account. grok_lead: Gene Wilder (born Jerome Silberman; June 11, 1933 â August 29, 2016) was an American actor, comedian, director, screenwriter, and author, renowned for his portrayals of eccentric, vulnerable, and neurotic characters in a career spanning over four decades. Best known for his iconic role as Willy Wonka in the 1971 musical fantasy film Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory, Wilder earned acclaim for his collaborations with directors like Mel Brooks and partners such as Richard Pryor, blending physical comedy with emotional depth. His work extended to Broadway, television, and literature, including directing four feature films and authoring a memoir, Kiss Me Like a Stranger: My Story (2005). Born in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, to a Russian-Jewish immigrant father, William Silberman, who manufactured novelty items, and Jeanne Baer, who suffered from rheumatic heart disease, Wilder adopted the stage name Gene Wilder in 1960, choosing 'Gene' after the protagonist of Thomas Wolfe's novel Look Homeward, Angel and 'Wilder' after playwright Thornton Wilder. His interest in acting ignited at age 13 after seeing a production of Death of a Salesman starring Lee J. Cobb, leading him to study at the University of Iowa's theater program, the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School in Englandâwhere he excelled in fencingâand later at the HB Studio and Actors Studio in New York under Lee Strasberg. After serving in the U.S. Army Medical Corps as a paramedic in the psychiatric unit at Valley Forge General Hospital in Pennsylvania, he began his professional stage career with an off-Broadway debut in Roots (1960) and a Broadway breakthrough in The Complaisant Lover (1961), for which he received the Clarence Derwent Award. Wilder's film career launched with a memorable supporting role as an undertaker in Arthur Penn's Bonnie and Clyde (1967), but he achieved stardom as the timid accountant Leo Bloom in Mel Brooks's The Producers (1968), earning an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor at age 35. He solidified his reputation in Brooks's Western parody Blazing Saddles (1974) as the gunslinger Waco Kid and in the horror-comedy Young Frankenstein (1974), which he co-wrote and directed, receiving another Oscar nomination for the screenplay. A frequent collaborator with Brooks and Woody Allen âappearing in Everything You Always Wanted to Know About Sex (1972)âWilder also formed a hit comedy duo with Richard Pryor in films like Silver Streak (1976) and Stir Crazy (1980), which grossed over $100 million combined and highlighted their interracial buddy dynamic. His directorial efforts included The Adventure of Sherlock Holmes ' Smarter Brother (1975), The World's Greatest Lover (1977), The Woman in Red (1984), and Haunted Honeymoon (1986), often starring himself alongside Gilda Radner, his third wife. In his later years, Wilder returned to television with a guest role on Will & Grace (2002â2003), winning a Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Guest Actor in a Comedy Series, and published novels such as My French Whore (2007) and Something to Remember You By (2013). Personally, he married four times: first to Mary Mercier (divorced), then to Mary Joan Schutz (divorced, adopting her daughter, Katharine), followed by comedian Gilda Radner from 1984 until her death from ovarian cancer in 1989, after which he co-founded Gilda's Clubs for cancer support; his fourth marriage was to Karen Boyer from 1991 until his death. Wilder battled non-Hodgkin's lymphoma in 1999 (achieving remission by 2005) and kept his Alzheimer's disease diagnosis private for three years before his passing on August 29, 2016, at his home in Stamford, Connecticut, at age 83. His legacy endures through his unique blend of whimsy and pathos, influencing generations of comic performers.
